entries.test: Comparative public evaluations of contemporary and earlier Turing Test systems would show whether contemporary systems have improved capabilities.
entries.note: The improvement claim has an empirical reading; the accompanying 'over' remark is rhetorical.
Whether the paper is convincing is an evaluative judgment without a stated evidentiary standard.
The central claim judges the adequacy of the bar and the legitimacy of declaring victory.
He asserts a claim about what the test measures. No shared operational distinction between gullibility and intelligence settles this categorical formulation.
'Nothing of lasting value' evaluates the worth of Goostman's contribution rather than specifying an absence of technical influence.
'Might' expresses a possibility conditional on a faceoff.

entries.test: The study's reported Turing Test results for ELIZA and ChatGPT in the no-persona condition would settle their relative performance.
entries.note: This is a concrete claim about reported experimental results.

entries.test: Public results comparing the same model with and without the specified persona prompt would establish whether the prompt was necessary for strong performance in the study.
entries.note: The normalization broadens 'the system' to LLMs and strengthens 'in no small part' into 'largely ... rather than intelligence.' The narrower prompt-dependence claim is testable.
Neither the audience's supposed estimate nor a comparable measure of actual intelligence is specified.

entries.test: Controlled public studies varying humanlike mannerisms while holding task competence fixed could show whether those mannerisms inflate users' intelligence judgments for these systems.
entries.note: 'Prey on' is reasonably read as a behavioral mechanism, without attributing conscious intent to the systems.
The recommendation cannot be settled empirically. The separate assertion about community opinion could be tested through representative surveys.

entries.test: Public evaluations of systems available at publication on complete Simpsons episodes and four seasons of Succession, including real-time explanations of deception and hallucination rates, would test the stated limitations.
entries.note: The normalization inserts 'likely' and replaces a specific four-season deception-comprehension task with following multiple seasons of any drama. 'I don't think they can' expresses a present capability judgment.

entries.test: Public benchmark releases and implementation reports available by publication would show whether anyone had fully implemented Marcus's proposed comprehension challenge.
entries.note: A documented complete implementation would falsify the claim.
'Might' makes the cost estimate explicitly tentative. The normalization turns two approximate alternative amounts into a range and omits the personal affordability claim.

entries.test: Public research budgets, investment announcements, and project portfolios of sufficiently funded AI organizations would show whether their spending prioritizes scaling.
entries.note: In context, preference has a plain reading as revealed research spending priorities.

entries.test: Results from a carefully implemented comprehension challenge comparing systems available on April 2, 2025 with human participants would settle whether any approached human performance.
entries.note: The wager is a firm conditional prediction. 'Current' fixes the systems to the publication date.

entries.test: Public comparisons with 2014 systems and evaluations of publication-era systems on reasoning, planning, and common-sense tasks would test improved mimicry and persistent capability gaps.
entries.note: The claim is broad but has a plain empirical reading about progress and remaining limitations.
Changing 'the measure' to 'a measure' strengthens the claim to deny any evidentiary value. The original gives no shared criterion for what qualifies as the measure of intelligence.
